title: Helidon 27 Introduces Restructured Programming Models and New Messaging and Data Modules
gist: Helidon 27, aligned with JDK 27, is the first release under Oracle's Tip & Tail library model, restructuring its programming models into Helidon Core (Imperative and Declarative), MicroProfile and Extensions, and adding Helidon Messaging and Helidon Data JDBC modules. Helidon 4.5.5 LTS continues as the stable Tail on a JDK 21 baseline.

insights.claim: Helidon 27 is the first Helidon release to follow Oracle's Tip & Tail Model of Library Development, in which the Tip adopts the latest Java technology and the Tail provides a more stable and secure baseline.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Signals Oracle-backed Java frameworks splitting into fast-moving and long-support tracks; watch adoption of the pattern across the Java Verified Portfolio.
insights.locator: The release of Helidon 27 is the very first

insights.claim: Helidon 27 is the Tip: it aligns with JDK 27, adopts the latest Java features and follows the OpenJDK release cadence, so Helidon 28 is expected with JDK 28 in March 2027.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Teams on the Tip track must plan upgrades every six months in lockstep with JDK releases.

insights.claim: Helidon 4.5.5 is the Tail: it keeps the Helidon 4.5 LTS on a JDK 21 baseline with JDK 25 support, prioritizing critical bugs, security fixes and selected backports for a longer-lived production baseline.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Risk-averse production teams can stay on the LTS without chasing JDK releases.

insights.claim: Helidon 27 is maintained under the Java Verified Portfolio, an Oracle-supported ecosystem first introduced at JavaOne 2026, alongside JavaFX 27, Jipher 20 and the Java Platform Extension for Visual Studio Code.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Shows Oracle consolidating supported Java tooling under one branded portfolio.
insights.locator: Helidon 27 is maintained under the auspices

insights.claim: Helidon Core replaces Helidon SE and offers two programming models: Imperative, which uses plain Java without dependency injection or annotations, and Declarative, which uses dependency injection and annotations that generate imperative code and wiring at build time.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Build-time wiring avoids runtime reflection overhead, which suits native-image and fast-startup microservices.
insights.locator: This release introduces the new Helidon Core

insights.claim: Helidon MicroProfile replaces the heritage Helidon MP, moves into its own project, and continues to support MicroProfile and Jakarta EE specifications under Helidon semantic versioning.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Existing MicroProfile and Jakarta EE users keep a migration path.
insights.locator: Helidon MicroProfile replaces the heritage Helidon MP

insights.claim: Helidon SE Integrations was moved to its own project and renamed Helidon Extensions, with each extension maintained under its own release lifecycle.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Decoupled lifecycles let integrations ship faster than the core.
insights.locator: Helidon SE Integrations has also been moved

themes.theme: New Messaging and Data JDBC modules

insights.claim: Helidon Messaging avoids reactive APIs such as the MicroProfile Reactive Messaging specification, letting developers use ordinary blocking Java with connector-neutral channels such as Kafka, JMS or Apache Pulsar bound through configuration and pluggable connectors.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: A deliberate move away from reactive programming toward simpler blocking code, consistent with the virtual-thread era.
insights.locator: Helidon Messaging, a new messaging layer

insights.claim: Helidon Data JDBC offers a unified repository-query API as an abstraction over traditional ORM, translating interfaces with query definitions into implementation classes at compile time, with support for Jakarta Persistence, EclipseLink and Hibernate ORM.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Compile-time repository generation competes with Micronaut Data-style approaches.
insights.locator: Helidon Data JDBC provides a unified API

insights.claim: The original Netty-based Helidon web server ran from version 1.0 to 3.0; a new web server, codenamed Helidon Nima and built on JEP 444 Virtual Threads, arrived with Helidon 4.0 in October 2023.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Helidon was an early framework adopter of virtual threads as its core server model.
insights.locator: The original Helidon web server, based on Netty

insights.claim: Helidon 3.0 (July 2022) required JDK 17, implemented MicroProfile 5.0 and selected Jakarta EE 9.1 specifications, and disabled deserialization by default via JEP 290.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Background on the project's security and baseline evolution.

insights.claim: Helidon was originally named J4C (Java for Cloud), launched Helidon SE in September 2018, and added a web client, database client and CLI in Helidon 2.0 in June 2020.
insights.speaker: Michael Redlich
insights.so_what: Context for how long the framework has been evolving.
